cards.name: OS-eDRAM: IGZO/IWO 2T0C gain-cell memory IP on a U.S. 200mm foundry
cards.what_it_is: A fabless IP company co-develops a low-temperature (<400C) IGZO or W-doped In2O3 2T0C gain-cell BEOL module with SkyWater (S130 in Bloomington MN, or the ex-Infineon Fab 25 in Austin, 130-65nm, 200mm). It then licenses the memory macro and compiler to ASIC designers, giving them on-die memory with ~4-5x the bit density of 130nm SRAM and near-zero standby leakage, stacked over logic.
cards.why_it_could_work: IGZO off-current ~3e-19 A/um gives >400-1,000 s retention (imec IEDM 2020/2021) vs SRAM's constant leakage, so an always-on edge chip can hold weights/activations at near-zero standby power. A planar 2T0C at ~30F2 is ~0.5 um2/bit at 130nm vs ~2.0-2.5 um2 for 6T SRAM [ESTIMATE], and because it sits in BEOL it uses no extra silicon area. Arbitrage: SkyWater bought Fab 25 (~$73M + working capital, ~400k wafer starts/yr) and is converting it to a foundry, so it needs differentiated process options. Embedded-memory IP royalties carry ~85% gross margin.

Competing embedded memories already at U.S. foundries: Weebit ReRAM (SkyWater S130), MRAM at GlobalFoundries.
cards.wins_axis: standby power per bit (W/Mb at idle) and on-die memory density vs SRAM at mature nodes
cards.buyer: Always-on edge-AI ASICs (keyword spotting, vision wake-up, sensor fusion) and DoD/onshore sensor ASICs on 130-65nm U.S. nodes that are SRAM-limited
cards.glut_reason: Priced against on-die SRAM/MRAM/ReRAM, not DDR5; a DDR5 price collapse does not change an ASIC's on-die memory choice.
cards.fatal_flaw: No U.S. foundry offers an oxide-semiconductor module. Qualifying one costs ~$10-30M and 3+ years [ESTIMATE], and PBTI lifetime was only ~1 year vs a 5-10 year target (imec 2021). ASIC teams rarely design in a single-source, unqualified memory when SkyWater already offers qualified ReRAM. SEL's patent estate is a freedom-to-operate risk.
cards.business_model_lenses: IP licensing; fabless->foundry; university/lab patent license (Georgia Tech/Notre Dame IWO, Purdue In2O3); defense-first
cards.founder_fit_note: Not as a solo founder: needs a device/process CTO and a SkyWater JDA. The founder could own BD and the software side (memory compiler GUI, characterization data portal).
cards.possible: yes - cells demonstrated on 300mm, oxide BEOL demonstrated on a U.S. 200mm line (Purdue)
cards.profitable: marginal - royalties on low-volume 130nm ASICs are small; the real money needs a 28nm-or-better foundry partner
cards.doable_by_founder: no - process-module development and reliability qualification are far beyond <$50k and a day job

cards.name: Standalone IGZO 2T0C DRAM die on a depreciated U.S. 200mm line (commodity DRAM substitute)
cards.what_it_is: Build discrete DRAM-substitute chips (DDR4/LPDDR-class interface) from four stacked IGZO 2T0C tiers over CMOS periphery on a depreciated U.S. 200mm 130nm line (SkyWater Fab 25 Austin) and sell them into the 2026 shortage. A capacitor-less, BEOL-stackable cell on cheap wafers is the whole pitch.
cards.why_it_could_work: No capacitor, low-temperature BEOL, and stackable tiers (IMECAS showed 4-layer 3D 2T0C with 400 s retention and 3 bits/cell at VLSI 2026), with depreciated 200mm wafers at ~$1-2.5K [ESTIMATE], while DDR5 sells for ~$27/GB. The scratch model kills it: ~0.0035 Gb/mm2 => ~7.6 GB per 200mm wafer => ~$336/GB including test and packaging, ~12x today's DDR5 price, ~31x the glut price and ~125x DDR5's estimated cost (~$2.7/GB). Even a hypothetical 300mm 28nm-class 4-tier version models at ~$11.8/GB, about the glut price and ~4x DRAM cost, and no U.S. foundry offers that line.

cards.name: IGZO memory printed on idle display-fab glass

cards.why_it_could_work: Display oxide-TFT lines are heavily depreciated and running underutilized (Omdia 2025). IGZO TFT leakage is tiny (SEL CAAC-IGZO <=200 zA), and a Gen 8.5 sheet is ~5.5 m2. Scratch model: at a ~2 um design rule a 2T0C cell is ~120 um2 => ~4e-6 Gb/mm2 => only ~2.3 GB per sheet => ~$266/GB before bonding, with microsecond access.

cards.name: U.S.-made HZO FeRAM family (1-16 Mb, rad-hard option) via SkyWater + Sandia
cards.what_it_is: A fabless company designs a family of hafnium-zirconium-oxide 1T1C FeRAM chips (SPI/QSPI and parallel, 1-16 Mb, plus rad-hard variants). The HZO capacitor module would be built on SkyWater's 130nm line (Bloomington MN or Fab 25 Austin), with rad-hard variants co-developed with or licensed from Sandia, which integrated HZO FeRAM into its trusted MESA fab at 200mm (May 2026). It sells an onshore second source to Infineon's PZT F-RAM.
cards.why_it_could_work: HZO is ALD-deposited and CMOS-friendly (no PZT lead contamination; ~2-3 extra masks, by analogy to TI's 2-mask FRAM on 130nm) and radiation hard (heavy-ion data; Sandia program). Space/defense F-RAM is close to sole-source (Infineon QML-V 2Mb). Wafers: ~$1,400 per 200mm [ESTIMATE]. This is a supply-security play, not a $/GB play: the scratch model is ~$770/GB because these are Mb-class parts.

cards.name: AlScN ferro-diode memory for 500-600C electronics (Penn/AFRL license + STTR)
cards.what_it_is: License Penn's AlScN ferroelectric-diode NVM (Jariwala/Olsson group, co-developed with AFRL) and build kB-to-Mb memory dies and high-temperature packaged modules for SiC electronics. Target uses are hypersonics, turbine-engine health monitoring, downhole geothermal/oil tools and Venus/space probes, entered through AFRL/DARPA SBIR-STTR contracts.
cards.why_it_could_work: Silicon DRAM and flash fail well below 300C [ESTIMATE]. Ni/Al0.68Sc0.32N/Pt diodes switched at 600C for >60 h at <15 V, which is compatible with SiC logic (Nature Electronics 2024), and scaled devices reach >100 Mbit/mm2 (arXiv 2025). The 2-terminal self-rectifying crossbar is a simple 3-4 mask BEOL. DoD keeps asking for this: AF254-D0806 (500C kB-scale NVM manufacturing scale-up) and DARPA DPA26BZ04-DV017 (-269 to +600C NVM, ~$1.2M Direct-to-Phase II, closed Aug 2026).

cards.name: Supercap-Killer PLP Kit (MRAM write-cache reference design)
cards.what_it_is: A licensed reference design (schematic/layout, FPGA or RISC-V controller RTL, Linux/Zephyr journaling driver, validation suite) that replaces the DRAM + supercapacitor power-loss-protection block in SSD, computational-storage, RAID/HBA and industrial data-logger boards with Everspin PERSYST 1Gb ST-DDR4 or 64-256Mb xSPI STT-MRAM. Parts come from Everspin (GF 28nm CMOS + Chandler AZ MTJ BEOL; Microchip Gresham OR line from 2H-2027); revenue is design-package fee + per-unit royalty + design-in services.
cards.why_it_could_work: IBM moved its 5th-gen FlashCore Module to Everspin MRAM instead of capacitors (Oct-2026) because supercaps/batteries wear out in a few years and take board space. The PLP block needs only 64-512 MB, so MRAM's ~30x $/bit penalty (~$100/Gb street vs ~$3/Gb DRAM) costs ~$50-400 per board but deletes the capacitor bank, hold-up circuitry and its field failures. DRAM write-cache cost doubled in 2026 while MRAM pricing did not move with the DRAM cycle, narrowing the delta. Everspin is adding U.S. capacity (Microchip 10-yr deal, up to 1,300 wafers/qtr).

Wafers come from SkyWater Fab 25 Austin TX (the ex-Cypress 200mm SRAM fab, 130-65nm), with U.S. assembly and test. Demand comes from long-lifecycle designs, not the DRAM cycle. Fab 25 made Cypress memory for decades and now runs as a foundry under an Infineon supply agreement. U.S.-fab provenance and longevity matter to DMSMS programs. ISSI is owned by China's Ingenic [UNVERIFIED-training].

cards.name: Compute-in-SRAM vector-search appliance on GSI Gemini APU
cards.subbranch: SRAM-at-scale: compute-in-SRAM as a DRAM-bandwidth substitute
cards.what_it_is: An on-prem retrieval and vector-search appliance plus software (FAISS/Milvus-compatible API, index build pipeline, monitoring) built on GSI Technology's Gemini APU PCIe cards. The APU does associative processing inside SRAM bit-lines (Gemini-I on TSMC 28nm, Gemini-II on 16nm) [UNVERIFIED-training]. It is sold to air-gapped defense/IC RAG and SIEM buyers as hardware plus an annual software subscription.
cards.why_it_could_work: The APU runs nearest-neighbour search inside SRAM, so a billion-vector index needs far less DRAM bandwidth and capacity per query than on CPUs/GPUs. With DRAM/HBM at 2-3x 2025 prices, DRAM GB per QPS matters. A 2025 Cornell study reported GPU-class retrieval at much lower energy [UNVERIFIED-training]. GSI is small (~$20M revenue) and needs software channel partners, and the integration is mostly software.

cards.subbranch: LLM inference KV-cache tiering - DRAM/CXL tier
cards.what_it_is: A 2U EPYC 9005 / Xeon 6 server (Supermicro or Dell OEM chassis) holding 3-6 TB of DDR5 plus E3.S CXL memory modules (Samsung CMM-D, Micron CZ122 or SK hynix CMM-DDR5), with 2x400G RDMA NICs. It ships with Mooncake Store / LMCache MP preconfigured to allocate KV on the CXL tier (/dev/dax). It is sold as a rack-shared 'KV memory node' that pools prefix and agent-session caches across GPU servers running vLLM/SGLang/Dynamo.
cards.why_it_could_work: KV is large: Llama-3.1-70B is 320 KiB/token at BF16 (40 GiB per 128k context); DeepSeek-V3 MLA is 68.6 KiB/token. Reloading a 128k context (20 GiB FP8) over 400G RDMA takes ~0.5 s, against ~41 s to recompute on one H100. Holding KV in DDR5 pays if a prefix is reused at least once every ~1.35 h at 4Q26 prices (~3.4 h in the glut). Mooncake reports 75% more requests within SLO at Kimi. vLLM requires the CPU tier as the staging tier, and LMCache/Mooncake already speak CXL /dev/dax.

cards.name: Memory FinOps Audit for Cloud SaaS
cards.what_it_is: A read-only web app with an AWS IAM role. It reads CUR plus CloudWatch-agent/Prometheus memory metrics across EC2 r/x/m-family, ElastiCache, RDS, K8s pods and JVM heaps. Output is a fixed-fee 'memory diet' report and a monitoring subscription, sold through AWS Marketplace to 20-500-engineer SaaS companies. The playbook levers are r->m family downsizing, K8s in-place pod resize (stable v1.35), JDK compact object headers and Redis->Valkey.
cards.why_it_could_work: AWS list prices put marginal RAM at $2.56-2.62/GiB-month, and RAM is 28-43% of the m7i/r7i list price (computed). Clusters leave about 18% of memory unused (Sysdig via KRR). Take a $40k/month EC2 bill with RAM at 30%, of which half the unused 18% is realizable: that saves about $1.1k/month, so a 25% share-of-savings fee is about $270/month. Reaching $20k MRR needs about 74 customers (d_calcs.py in D_notes).

cards.founder_fit_note: Yes. Web app plus AWS APIs is the founder's home turf at T0, but the moat is weak.

cards.name: Fleet Memory-Reclaim Autopilot (TMO for on-prem)
cards.subbranch: Transparent memory compression / proactive reclaim / dedup
cards.what_it_is: A per-node agent plus web control plane. It enables and tunes upstream Linux zswap (zsmalloc + zstd/lz4), Meta-Senpai-style PSI-driven proactive reclaim via cgroup2, KSM page dedup on Proxmox/KVM hosts, and Kubernetes 1.34 LimitedSwap, with per-workload SLO guardrails and a 'GB reclaimed = $ of DRAM not bought' ledger. It is sold per node to on-prem/colo operators who buy DRAM at 2026 prices.
cards.why_it_could_work: On-prem buyers pay DRAM directly: $14-16/GB at contract, ~$32/GB street (64GB RDIMM $900-1,000 to $2,064). Take a 200-server x 512GB fleet with 20% cold memory at ~2:1 compression: it frees ~10 TB, which defers $154k (contract) to $328k (street) of DRAM. Kubernetes container swap went stable in v1.34, removing the old 'kubelet refuses swap' blocker. Meta reported 20-32% fleet memory savings from TMO [UNVERIFIED-T: paper not opened].

The cloud K8s optimizers (CAST AI, ScaleOps) focus on requests and instances, not swap [ESTIMATE]. MemVerge left the field.
cards.wins_axis: Effective $/GB (usable GB per purchased GB), which defers DRAM capex
cards.buyer: Regional hosting providers, MSPs running Proxmox/KVM, on-prem Kubernetes and CI/build farms, and university HPC centers that must buy DDR5 RDIMMs at 2026 prices

cards.fatal_flaw: It is configuration of free kernel features. Sophisticated operators already do it themselves, and conservative ones fear swap latency and OOM incidents. One production incident at an early customer ends the company.
cards.founder_fit_note: Marginal. The control plane is easy for him; safe Linux memory-management tuning needs a kernel-savvy contractor or co-founder.
cards.possible: yes - production-proven at Meta/Google, and every component is upstream
cards.profitable: marginal - real savings while DRAM is expensive, but buyers can DIY and the pain halves in a glut
cards.doable_by_founder: marginal - needs a Linux-mm expert for SLO safety; the sales cycle to on-prem ops is slow

cards.name: KV-Cache Tier Integration & Tuning for Self-Hosted LLMs
cards.what_it_is: A productized integration service plus a benchmarking/monitoring dashboard. It deploys host-DRAM and NVMe KV-cache tiers (LMCache, NVIDIA Dynamo KVBM, Mooncake Store, SGLang HiCache) into mid-market vLLM/SGLang clusters and sizes the DRAM tier per workload from measured prefix-reuse rates. Recurring revenue comes from hit-rate, TTFT and $/token monitoring.
cards.why_it_could_work: Llama-3.1-70B needs 320 KiB of KV per token, so 1 TB of host DRAM ($15k at 2026 contract) holds ~3.1M reusable prefix tokens. Mooncake reports Kimi serving 75% more requests within SLO, and Dynamo claims 2x TTFT from KV-aware routing. The stacks churn fast (LMCache shipped 65 PyPI releases from May 2025 to Oct 2026; vLLM 0.32.0 came out 2026-10-18), and teams running 8-64 GPUs lack staff to keep up.

cards.name: Memory Cost Escalation Index + EPA clause kit
cards.what_it_is: Publish a monthly, methodology-documented memory cost index family (DDR4, DDR5, LPDDR4X/5X, eMMC/NAND). It is computed from authorized-distributor quote APIs (Nexar/Octopart, DigiKey, Mouser) plus transaction data contributed by a marketplace partner such as Mobius Materials. License it with ready-to-use economic-price-adjustment (EPA) clauses and a calculator API, so system integrators, EMS houses and federal contractors can pass memory cost through in both directions, like steel and copper surcharges. Federal contracts already allow index-based material EPA (FAR 16.203-1(a)(3), FAR 52.216-4).

Fixed-price deals for servers, industrial PCs and embedded systems either bleed or carry fat contingencies; Samsung's own device division lost money on component costs in 3Q26. A neutral index lets both sides drop the contingency. Example (e_estimates §11): memory is 35% of a $500k deliverable, so +25% memory triggers a +$43.75k adjustment and -60% a -$105k refund. Revenue: 30 x $6k + 5 x $24k = $300k ARR at 89% GM if self-built, 57% if a contract-price feed must be licensed.
